tagline: Western Chesapeake towns tell a story of ferries, steamships and beach trains.
intro: Roots and Tides links Annapolis with communities along the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay, following several roads rather than a single highway. The Maryland scenic byway connects historic London Town, Galesville and the former resorts of North Beach and Chesapeake Beach. Along the route, the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center occupies a landscape of coastal plain forest, farmland, wetlands and marshes. Scientists there study how forests, farms and coasts function, using long-term experiments and global data to inform decisions from the local to international scale.

Earlier journeys depended on different connections: William Brown’s tavern at London Town stood beside his South River ferry, on the road between Williamsburg and Philadelphia. Galesville later served as a steamship terminus for Annapolis and Baltimore. At Chesapeake Beach, Otto Mears built a railway to bring Washington travelers to a shoreline resort. The automobile’s rise and the Great Depression undermined that business; the last beach train departed in 1935.

Driving south from Annapolis brings you first to London Town, then past the research center to Galesville. Continue west of Herring Bay and through Fairhaven before reaching North Beach and Chesapeake Beach. The route continues south through Willows, then turns toward Plum Point on the bay.

moments.title: Historic London Town
moments.text: William Brown built his brick tavern beside a ferry he owned on the South River. Completed in 1764, it served a road linking Williamsburg and Philadelphia, but the expensive house helped put Brown in debt. He eventually conveyed it to his lender’s estate. The county acquired the building in 1828 and used it as an almshouse until 1965. Now a museum, the two-story house has a chimney at each end of its cut-off hipped roof. Other period buildings in the London Town park are reconstructions. A central pavilion projects from the facade, with brick and stone steps leading up to the entrance.

moments.title: Galesville
moments.text: The West River connected Galesville to Annapolis and Baltimore by steamship. The town was a terminus on that line and a home to Chesapeake Bay watermen and their families. Its boating economy has since developed a leisure trade. The community’s history also reaches back to early Quaker settlement and the West River Friends meeting. Galesville occupies the river’s western shore, on an arm of the Chesapeake.

moments.title: Chesapeake Beach
moments.text: Chesapeake Beach’s 1898 railway station preserves a change in how people reached the bay. Otto Mears and his partners developed hotels, beaches, casinos and a boardwalk for their resort. African-American workers carried out most of the railway’s construction and maintenance, even as its passenger facilities enforced racial separation. Cars and the Great Depression cut into business, and the last train left on April 15, 1935. The station became a museum in 1979. Exhibits interpret both the railway and the town’s local history. Its two low, hip-roofed sections include a former open boarding area later enclosed for storage.
